[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mAs the Moon orbits Earth, its gravity pulls on the water in the oceans, creating a bulge of water on the side of Earth
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mfacing the Moon. On the opposite side of Earth, a second bulge forms not because of a direct pull, but because the
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mMoon pulls Earth itself more strongly than it pulls the distant water on the far side. In effect, water on the near
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mside is pulled toward the Moon, while water on the far side is left behind. Earth rotates through these two bulges
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252meach day, so most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides in a period of about 24 hours and 50
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mminutes. That extra 50 minutes reflects the fact that the Moon moves a little in its orbit each day, so Earth must
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mrotate a bit further to bring the same location back under the Moon.

[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mThe Sun also creates tides, though smaller. When the Sun, Earth, and Moon are aligned at new moon and full moon, their
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mtidal bulges reinforce each other and produce higher high tides and lower low tides, known as spring tides. The term
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mhas nothing to do with the season, but comes from the idea of tides springing forth. When the Moon is at first or
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mthird quarter and forms a right angle with the Sun as seen from Earth, the solar and lunar bulges partially cancel
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252meach other, resulting in more moderate tides called neap tides.

[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mThe simple picture of two bulges following the Moon is modified greatly by geography. Continents block the free
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mmovement of water, ocean basins have their own natural resonant frequencies, and the Coriolis effect from Earth's
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mrotation deflects moving water. As a result, tides do not appear as vast traveling bulges but as complex rotating wave
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252msystems that sweep around ocean basins. In some enclosed seas the tidal range may be less than a foot, while in
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mfunnel-shaped bays such as the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water can rise more than 50 feet between low and high tide.

[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mPredicting tides requires accounting for all of these factors, and coastal communities have done so for centuries for
[38;5;242m  [38;5;252mnavigation, fishing, and flood protection.
